title: Dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier
body: Some reactions run both ways at once. In this tube, brown nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) molecules pair up to make colourless dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄). At the same time, other N₂O₄ molecules split back apart.

At equilibrium, both reactions run at the same rate, so the colour stays steady. But nothing has stopped. Molecules keep pairing up and splitting, in balance. Picture walking up a down escalator at exactly its speed. You stay in one place, yet you keep moving. That's a dynamic equilibrium.

Le Chatelier's principle: change the conditions, and the balance shifts to fight the change. Pairing up gives out heat. So heating the tube favours splitting apart: more brown NO₂ and a darker colour. Cooling favours pairing up, so the gas turns paler.
equation: 2NO₂ (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄ (colourless), ΔH = −57 kJ/mol (pairing up gives out heat)
realWorld: The Haber process makes ammonia for fertiliser, and it's an equilibrium too. Factories pick a temperature and pressure that push the balance towards ammonia. They also keep the reaction fast enough to be worth running.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, §13.3 Shifting Equilibria: Le Châtelier’s Principle. https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/13-3-shifting-equilibria-le-chateliers-principle
